source: Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (Proc. Human Factors Soc.)
finding: Original abstract opened through the Crossref record. Fireground commanders were studied by critical incident protocol analysis. In under 12% of decision points was there any evidence of comparing two or more options at once. Most of the time they recognised the situation as typical and picked the matching action.
numbers: Abstract: comparison of 2+ options in less than 12% of decision points. Sample size is NOT in the abstract. Secondary web summaries give 26 commanders (mean about 23 years service) and 156 decision points; one Q&A snippet says 28 of 156 (about 18%) involved more than one option. Those are unverified and conflict with the 12% figure.
quote: in less than 12% of the decision points was there any evidence of simultaneous comparisons and relative evaluation of two or more options
limits: Only the abstract was read; the full 1986 paper was behind a 403 and the DTIC report returned a web page, not a PDF. The sample numbers are secondary. Fire commanders are experts in a familiar domain; the study has no outcome-quality measure, so it shows what experts do, not that it is better.
agent_relevance: Fix for gap 3: the safe citable number is 'under 12% of decision points showed option comparison', not '80% single option' from memory. Do not cite N=26 or 156 as verified.

source: Fire Engineering article citing Klein, Calderwood, Clinton-Cirocco (1988) ARI Technical Report 796
finding: A trade article on fireground command cites the 1988 ARI report for the claim that in 80 percent of incidents the commander handled decision points without considering more than one option.
numbers: 80 percent of incidents (as stated by the article). The article gives no commander count, decision-point count, or comparison share.
limits: Secondary source, third-hand. The 80% is per incident in this article, while the 1986 abstract's under 12% is per decision point. These are different units and must not be merged. NIST record confirms report ARI-TR-796, June 1988, 112 pages, but gives no figures.
agent_relevance: Shows the 'about 80% single option' number in circulation is a different measure from the abstract's 12%. Cite the unit with the number.

source: Klein, Wolf, Militello, Zsambok (1995) Characteristics of skilled option generation in chess (OBHDP 62:63-69)
finding: Not opened. Crossref has no abstract. Secondary summaries (web search; Military Review 2004) say the first moves chess players generated were much better than chance, experts generated about 3 to 5 moves, and a later paper says the expert advantage in first-move and final-move strength was non-significant because the sample was small.
numbers: No verified numbers. Secondary: 3 to 5 moves per expert; expert advantage non-significant (small N).
limits: Do not cite figures. The original must be opened before any number is used. Chess has a fast, rule-bound, fully-known state, unlike COA planning.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open for this paper. The 'first option is good' claim is supported in direction only.

source: Johnson and Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices (OBHDP 91:215-229)
finding: Not opened (no abstract in Crossref or RePEc). Secondary summaries: handball players watched video clips, rated option quality fell as more options were generated, and players were more likely to switch from a good first option to a poor final choice than the reverse.
numbers: Secondary only: 85 male handball players (Germany and Brazil, six clubs, medium skill). No effect sizes verified.
limits: A systematic review calls the sample medium-skill, not elite. Option quality was judged by experts, not by game outcome. A 2004 Military Review article (opened, d06) describes the same result: later COAs were of significantly lower quality than the first for skilled decision makers.
agent_relevance: Direction supported by two secondary readings; size unknown. Treat 'first option is best' as a hypothesis for experts in familiar tasks, not a rule.

source: Raab, Klenk, Medvegy et al. (2026) Intuitive choices in chess option-generation are task and expertise dependent: a conceptual replication (Journal of Expertise 9:58+)
finding: Conceptual replication of Medvegy et al. (2022) in chess with a larger and weaker sample. Players generated few options and often chose the first, but the first option did NOT have a clear quality edge over later options. The take-the-first advantage seems to need higher expertise. Intuitive choices were not worse than deliberate ones. Tactical positions under time pressure were the weak spot.
numbers: N = 92 (original N = 34); mean rating below 2000 (original had a group above 2000). Mean 2.2 options generated. First generated move picked as best in 37.3% of cases. Repeated-measures ANOVA of move quality by serial position (first to fourth): F(3, 992) = 1.73, p = .159 (not significant), though the first option was descriptively higher. Blitz rating correlated with move quality in position 1, r = .356.
quote: unlike the original study, lower-rated players did not show a clear quality advantage of the first generated option
limits: Partial replication: direction held, magnitude did not. Positions were four static diagrams, quality rated by experts and engines, no game outcomes. Online ratings were mixed with official ones.
agent_relevance: Main boundary condition for gap 3: first-option quality depends on expertise. A base LLM is not an expert in a novel military scenario, so 'take the first plan' has no support there.

source: Ross, Klein, Thunholm, Schmitt, Baxter (2004) The recognition-primed decision model (Military Review, Jul-Aug)
finding: Army-journal review by Klein and Thunholm. It states research support is weak for the MDMP assumption that developing and comparing several COAs finds a better COA. It reports Thunholm's Swedish division-level planning-group experiment: a recognitional planning model (one COA, then wargame and refine) against the Swedish MDMP variant.
numbers: Recognitional model gave about 20% faster planning tempo. Plans were 'somewhat bolder and better adapted' than MDMP plans. Participants estimated it took at least 30% less time. No effect sizes, no group counts, no blind quality score in this article.
quote: Research support is weak for the MDMP's basic assumption that developing and comparing several COAs results in finding a superior COA.
limits: Written by the model's own authors, so not independent. The quality claim is qualitative. Authors admit commanders without experience of the mission produce weaker plans under either method. Primary Thunholm reports not opened.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 4 in part: no outcome-validity data for the multi-COA/five-test screen was found; the best field comparison favours one COA plus wargame on speed, with only soft evidence on quality.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: temporal perspective in the explanation of events (JBDM 2:25-38)
finding: Abstract opened through Crossref. The paper defines prospective hindsight (explain a future event as if it already happened). In experiment 1, temporal perspective (future vs past) showed little influence; whether the outcome was certain or uncertain strongly changed the type of explanation. Experiment 2 supports that uncertainty changes the explanation type, not the time spent.
numbers: Abstract gives no percentages. Secondary: 76 MBA students and 32 nonstudent adults in the second experiment. The popular '30% more reasons' figure is NOT in the abstract and could not be confirmed.
limits: Only the abstract was read. The abstract does not state a prospective-hindsight benefit; the famous 30% claim may come from the full text or may be a citation drift. Treat it as unverified.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the key premortem origin paper does not, in its abstract, report the effect the premortem literature quotes. Do not use the 30% number.

source: Schwenk (1990) Effects of devil's advocacy and dialectical inquiry on decision making: a meta-analysis (OBHDP 47:161-176)
finding: Not opened (ScienceDirect paywall; Crossref and RePEc have no abstract). Search-result abstract text says devil's advocacy was more effective than the expert-only approach in general; dialectical inquiry was not shown better than expert-only on ill-structured tasks; neither was shown to be the better way to add conflict.
numbers: No study count or effect size verified.
limits: Abstract-level summary only. The underlying studies are lab tasks with students, mostly structured case problems. Dissent method effects were mixed.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 old-source side stays open. The direction (a forced critic helps vs consensus) is plausible; size unknown.

source: Peabody (2017) Improving planning: quantitative evaluation of the premortem technique in field and laboratory settings (MTU master's thesis)
finding: Thesis abstract opened. Experiment 1 (field): ROTC cadet teams did six time-limited field exercises, half with a premortem and half with their usual plan check. With the premortem there were fewer fouls and less fixation, with no extra time. Experiment 2: premortem vs worst-case-scenario prompt gave no difference in the count of reasons and solutions but different kinds. Experiment 3: premortem gave more reasons than worst-case; groups gave more solutions than individuals.
numbers: Exp 1: 52 cadets (a blog summary says 48), 6 exercises, within-team design. Exp 2: 72 individuals. Exp 3: 82 participants. No effect sizes or error counts in the abstract.
limits: Unpublished thesis, abstract only. Small samples, short tasks, a worst-case control that is itself a risk prompt. Count of reasons is not plan success.
agent_relevance: Best controlled human premortem data found. Suggests a premortem step costs little time and can cut errors, but the advantage over a plain 'what could go wrong' prompt is not shown (Exp 2).

source: Kim, Kim, Park, Park, Breazeal, McDuff, Park (2025/2026) InvThink: premortem reasoning for safer language models (arXiv 2510.01569v3)
finding: A prompting and training method that makes the model list possible harms, analyse them, then answer under constraints. It is called a premortem. Safety gains grow with model size. The task is safety, not planning.
numbers: TRIDENT professional-ethics harmfulness 3.22 (zero-shot) to 2.19 (InvThink prompting), a 32.0% cut; SafetyPrompt got 2.62. Agentic misalignment: blackmail rate down 90% and murder-attempt rate down 44% on average (prompting variants). Reasoning benchmarks: up to +5.0% on GPQA and MATH500 for the SFT+RL variant.
limits: Safety outcomes judged by LLM judges (cross-judge exact agreement 76.7% for InvThink). Not a planning or COA task. No equal-token control against a plain 'think about risks' prompt of the same length is reported in what I read. Some numbers come from fine-tuned variants, not prompting alone.
agent_relevance: Closest 2025-2026 LLM test of a premortem structure. It supports 'enumerate failure modes first' as a cheap prompt. It does not show better plans.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Devil's Advocate: anticipatory reflection for LLM agents (arXiv 2405.16334)
finding: Before each action the GPT-4 agent asks itself what could go wrong and what the fallback is, then revises the plan if an action fails. Tested on WebArena.
numbers: Success rate after seven episodes: anticipatory reflection 23.5%, tree-search LATS 22.7%, Plan+Act with post-failure reflection 19.8%. Plan revisions per task: 0.64 vs 1.16 (LATS) vs 2.03 (Plan+Act), a 45% cut. Actions in last trial: 7.07 vs 4.47 for Plan+Act.
limits: Gap to LATS is 0.8 points, probably inside noise; no confidence intervals or seeds reported in the text I read. Web navigation, not military planning. Token cost not compared at equal budget, although the agent spends more calls per step.
agent_relevance: A self-run 'devil's advocate' step is a possible small gain on a long-horizon agent task, at extra calls. Fits the guardrail idea of a failure check before action but is not strong evidence.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Stafford, Collier, Vlachos (2025) Conformity in large language models (arXiv 2410.12428v2)
finding: All tested models conform to a majority, more so when unsure. Adding one dissenting voice (a devil's advocate that gives a different answer) cut conformity, even when that dissenter was also wrong. Instruction-tuned models conformed less.
numbers: Correlation between task accuracy and conformity -0.777 on MMLU-based tasks. DA effect strong for Gemma2 and Llama3, weaker for Mistral and Qwen2. Effective on subjective question sets too. Exact percentages are in figures I did not transcribe.
limits: Small open models (7B to 9B), multiple-choice questions, a confederate-style setup. This is about resisting social pressure, not about improving a plan.
agent_relevance: Shows why a devil's advocate may work in a multi-agent loop: dissent breaks agreement. Also explains the 'harmonious dialog' failure (K23): without forced dissent the agents just agree.

source: Ke et al. (2024) Enhancing diagnostic accuracy through multi-agent conversations: LLMs to mitigate cognitive bias (arXiv 2401.14589)
finding: Four GPT-4 agents (decider, devil's advocate, facilitator, recorder) discussed 16 case reports where cognitive bias had caused misdiagnosis. The initial answer was wrong in every run; after the discussion most runs reached the right diagnosis.
numbers: 80 simulations. Initial diagnosis accuracy 0/80 (0%). After discussion, top diagnosis correct 57/80 (71.3%); correct in final two 64/80 (80.0%).
limits: No control without the devil's advocate role, no single-agent re-ask baseline, and the 0% start was built by choosing biased cases. Cannot tell what the devil's advocate itself added. Medical cases, not plans.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. It shows a multi-role loop can recover from a planted wrong answer, but not that the critic role is the cause.

source: Wang, Cassano, Wu et al. (2024) Planning in natural language improves LLM search for code generation: PlanSearch (arXiv 2409.03733)
finding: Searching over diverse natural-language plans (observations, then plans, then code) beats repeated sampling of code, because repeated samples are near-duplicates. Diversity measured in idea space predicts how much search helps.
numbers: LiveCodeBench, Claude 3.5 Sonnet: pass@1 41.4%, repeated-sampling pass@200 60.6%, PlanSearch pass@200 77.0%. PlanSearch often LOWERS pass@1. Public-test filtering cuts samples about tenfold (pass@20 77.1% vs unfiltered pass@200 77.0%); that tenfold gain is from filtering, not planning. Per-idea solve rates polarise to 0% or 100%.
limits: Code with unit tests as an external verifier, which COA planning lacks. Compares equal numbers of samples (pass@k), not equal tokens; PlanSearch calls cost more tokens per sample. Diversity score is an LLM-judge measure.
agent_relevance: Best evidence for gap 7: forced plan-level diversity beat plain resampling when a verifier exists, and near-duplicate candidates are the failure. Without an outside verifier the gain is unproven.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: Compares parallel best-of-N, sequential self-revision, and verifier-guided search at matched compute. On easier problems, sequential revision is the better use of compute; on harder problems needing different high-level approaches, parallel resampling or tree search is better. A difficulty-adaptive split beats best-of-N.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N using about 4x less test-time compute (revisions and search). FLOPs-matched comparison against a 14x larger model is also reported (math tasks, MATH benchmark, PaLM 2 variants).
limits: Maths problems with a trained verifier (process reward model). No planning or adversarial task. The revision model was fine-tuned for revising.
agent_relevance: Nearest equal-compute test for gap 1. Fits our schema: use few high-level alternatives on hard, open problems and revise on easy ones. No source tests 3 COAs vs plan-plus-self-check on a planning task, so gap 1 stays open.

source: Wang, Todd, Xiao, Yuan, Cote, Clark, Jansen (2024) Can language models serve as text-based world simulators? (arXiv 2406.06485)
finding: GPT-4 was asked to predict the next state after an action in text games. It is an unreliable simulator: it fails on changes not caused by the agent's action and on steps needing arithmetic, common sense, or science.
numbers: Best accuracy on non-trivial state changes 59.9%. Game-progress prediction 92.1% with game rules in context, 61.5% without. Humans 80% vs sampled GPT-4 50% in a normalised human study. 2954 test transitions. The authors note that at modest single-step accuracy, errors compound, so a long rollout would be right 1% of the time or less.
limits: GPT-4 (2023-24 model) in text games with JSON state, not combat adjudication. Newer models were not tested here.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: direct evidence against an LLM replacing a simulator for multi-step outcome prediction. Use an LLM judge only for single-step checks, with an external rule check for state.

source: Xu, Cui, Wang, Xu, Wang (2025) Strategy-augmented planning for LLMs via opponent exploitation (arXiv 2505.08459)
finding: In MicroRTS, an LLM that picks from a strategy library using a trained Strategy Evaluation Network, which predicts the win chance of each strategy against the observed opponent, beats plain LLM planning by a wide margin and matches RL methods.
numbers: Reported: 85.35% improvement over the text-action planning baseline (TA) averaged across opponents; the table shows vanilla-LLM and CoT planning winning 0% to 25% in several matchups where SAP wins 95% to 100% (win rates read from a garbled table). SEN false-positive rate and 93.3% best-response win rate against one opponent also reported.
limits: The opponent model is a separately trained network, not the LLM. Opponents are scripted bots in a small real-time game. Gain is from learned opponent evaluation.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6: an opponent model helps, but it was a trained module, not a prompted LLM. No test of an untrained LLM opponent model beating static ranking was found.

source: Yao et al. (2025) SPIN-Bench: how well do LLMs plan strategically and reason socially? (arXiv 2503.12349, COLM 2025)
finding: Multi-domain test mixing PDDL planning, board games, cooperative cards, and negotiation. LLMs plan well in short single-agent tasks but break down on deep multi-hop search and on playing against opponents.
numbers: In Connect Four and Chess, every LLM lost 100% of matches to solver-level engines (Stockfish level 0 was already too strong). o1 sustained 100% accuracy on spatial tracking up to 29 steps; mean factual-tracking accuracy was 94.3% for o1, 56.3% o1-mini, 41.7% GPT-4o.
limits: Games with clean rules, not military planning. Test models are 2024 to early 2025.
agent_relevance: Supports the view that LLM look-ahead against an adversary is weak, so opponent modelling should be given structure and external tools (gap 6).

source: Echterhoff, Liu, Alessa, McAuley, He (2024) Cognitive bias in decision-making with LLMs: BiasBuster (arXiv 2403.00811)
finding: Tests anchoring, framing, status quo, primacy, group attribution and sequential biases on admissions-style decisions, and shows LLMs show human-like biases outside geopolitics. A self-help prompt in which the model rewrites its own biased prompt cut bias best.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students when the same case was framed as 'reject'; Llama-2 7B classified 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Self-help left 0% of biased group-attribution elements for GPT-4 and 2.7% for framing. Few-shot debiasing sometimes made things worse.
limits: Admissions and similar decisions, not plans. 2023-24 models; evaluation was cut to 400 prompts per experiment to save cost.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: framing and anchoring biases do carry to non-geopolitical choices, so a plan-selection step should present candidates in randomised order and neutral framing. Escalation bias on plan selection is still untested.

source: Search record: COA-GPT replications and token cost (web search, arXiv 2511.10651 opened)
finding: No independent replication of COA-GPT on a different simulator was found. The Nov 2025 paper that cites it (2511.10651) is about LLM report generation for simulation deduction, not COA generation, and reports no COA results. Park et al. 2026 (2604.20862, already a12) is an architecture paper. COA-GPT reports speed in seconds but no token or dollar cost in what was found.
numbers: No numbers. 2511.10651 gives only a rubric-scored report-quality comparison to a baseline method.
limits: A negative search result, not proof of absence. Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex citation APIs were rate-limited, so the citing-paper list is incomplete.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open. Treat K03 as single-source.
